division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.1   In this Part,
(a) “assessment officer” means the court clerk for the judicial
centre in which the action is located;
(b) “review officer” means an assessment officer who, in the
opinion of the clerk of the Court, has for the purpose of
reviewing contingency fee or retainer agreements and
lawyers’ charges
(i) an acceptable degree in law, and
(ii) sufficient experience in the practice of law,
and who is designated as a review officer by
(iii) the clerk of the Court for the judicial centre in which
the action is located, or
(iv) if there is no clerk of the Court for the judicial centre
in which the action is located, the Minister.

BOOK_B.title: Definitions

commentary.text: Rule 10.1 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.1. In Shreem Holdings Inc. v. Barr Picard, 2014 ABQB 112, 2014 CarswellAlta 313, 100 Alta. L.R. (5th) 314, Mr. Justice Wakeling said, at paragraphs 66–67: 66 I am satisfied that Part 10, Division 1 of the Alberta Rules of Court constitutes a comprehensive code of a discrete subject matter—the review of a lawyer's charges outside the confines of an action for unpaid charges. This unit determines the amount which a lawyer may charge her client and the obligations a client has to her lawyer. It assigns particular tasks to different adjudicators and determines who may apply for a review, what may be done with the certificate of review and the consequences of a review being initiated. This regime occupies the field and leaves no room for the Court to exercise its inherent jurisdiction and order that the first question be answered through a hearing process. 67 The existence of a comprehensive protocol in the Alberta Rules of Court on a discrete topic is a clear indication on the part of the legislature and the judges of the superior courts20 of Alberta that any matter covered by the comprehensive code is to be governed by the applicable rule and not the court's inherent jurisdiction. Re Stelco Inc., 196 O.A.C. 142, 152 (C.A. 2005) &Etri Fans Ltd. v. N.M.B. (U.K.) Ltd., [1987] 1 W.L.R. 1110, 1114 (C.A). [Footnote omitted] In Rath & Co. v. Sweetgrass First Nation, 2013 ABQB 165, 2013 CarswellAlta 399, 559 A.R. 12, 85 Alta. L.R. (5th) 219, Justice Tilleman discussed the new terminology. At paragraph 22, his Lordship said: 22 Despite the new Rules, the old jurisprudence remains instructive. The change in name from “taxing officer” under the old Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/1968 [Old Rules] to “review officer” under the new Rules is consistent with the goal of increasing usability and simplifying complex language: Alberta Law Reform Institute, Rules of Court Project, Final Report No 95 (Edmonton: ALRI, 2008) at para 9. In that report's rule concordance table, there is consistency that old rules regarding “taxation” concord with new rules regarding “review.” In Champagne v. Sidorsky, 2012 ABQB 522 at para 26, 220 ACWS (3d) 708 [Champagne], Justice Jones found “that the term ‘litigation representative’ under the Rules replaces and is inclusive of ‘next friend’ and ‘guardian ad litem’ under the Old Rules”. Likewise, I find that a “review officer” replaces a “taxing officer” and a “review” replaces a “taxation.”

see_also: Official text (searched for 'rule 10.1', 'Rules 10.1', line-wrapped forms and form headings '[Rule 10.x]'): no rule or form cites 10.1 by number; the only hits are the table of contents (line 1458) and the rule itself (line 11621, pdf pp.192-193: (a) on p.192, (b) on p.193 after the running head 'Rule 10.2'). By subject: the Appendix (Definitions) defines the same two terms in the same words - 'assessment officer' (line 40564, pdf p.668) and 'review officer' (line 41073, pdf pp.676-677; its sub-items are lettered (a)-(b) and (c)-(d) where 10.1 has (i)-(ii) and (iii)-(iv)); the terms are used in 9.35(1)(b) (line 11238), 13.33 (line 17400), 10.9, 10.13, 10.34, 10.36 and the rest of Division 1-2, Schedule B item 6 of Division 1 ('appointment for review by a review officer', line 39408) and the forms for reviews and assessments (Form 42 '[Rule 10.13]', Form 43 '[Rule 10.26]', Form 44 '[Rule 10.35(1)]', Form 45 '[Rule 10.37]', Form 46 '[Rule 10.44]').

BOOK_A (all Book A files searched, line-wrapped forms included; pages from the 'N-NN' markers of combined_rule10.txt): the rule text is at p.10-3 (lines 52-66, running head 'R.10.1' line 47, DIVISION 1 heading lines 48-50); Book A prints no information note, related provisions or commentary for 10.1. The Part introduction (lines 22-41, before the first page marker) lists 'assessment officer' and 'review officer' among the words 'that have defined meanings in the Appendix'. Book A pointers that name 10.1: (1) p.10-5 (line 175, in the 10.2 note E 'Security for Fees'): 'Fewer lawyers are familiar with R.10.1(2) or the possibility of taking other security' - FLAG: official 10.1 has no subrule (2); the official subrule about security is 10.2(2) ('A lawyer may be paid in advance or take security for future lawyer's charges'); the sources do not say which was meant. (2) p.10-8 (line 308, Related Provisions of 10.4): '10.1(2) (agreement to provide security)' - FLAG: same, no 10.1(2) in the official text; the label matches 10.2(2). (3) p.10-35 (line 1694, in the 10.19 note): 'On negligence by the lawyer, see R.10.1 and commentary, supra.' - FLAG: 10.1 is the definitions rule and carries no commentary on negligence; the note on negligence and set-off is in Book A's 10.2 note (Part C 'Misconduct', p.10-5); the sources do not say which rule was meant. (4) p.10-96 (line 5125, footnote 5 in the 10.31 note): 'The test is reasonableness in prosecuting the suit, not R.10.1' - FLAG: 10.1 states no test of reasonableness (10.2(1) does); the sources do not say which rule was meant, but the same decision, McAteer v. Devoncroft Dev. (#2) 2003 ABQB 425, 340 AR 1, is cited in Book A's 10.2 note (p.10-6, footnote 8) for 'Rule 10.2 does not apply to the question of costs to the opponent on a solicitor-client (full indemnity) basis'.
